Ailuravus.note: A squirrel-like early rodent nearly a metre long with its bushy tail, preserved at Messel with leaves in its gut.

Anthropornis.note: A giant penguin of the Eocene of Antarctica, 1.7 metres tall and up to 90 kilograms, with a bend in its flipper bone.

Apidium.note: A squirrel-monkey-sized early anthropoid of the Fayum, a leaper in the trees that fringed the Oligocene rivers.

Archaeotherium.note: A cow-sized entelodont, a 'hell pig' of the Oligocene plains; bite marks show it stored the carcasses of early camels to eat later.

Arctocyon.note: A bear-sized arctocyonid with blunt teeth and a heavy tail -- an omnivore of the Paleocene forests on both sides of the North Atlantic.

Bemalambda.note: A dog-sized pantodont of the earliest Paleocene of South China, one of the first mammals to take over the plant-eating roles the dinosaurs had left.

Borealosuchus.note: A long-snouted crocodilian that crossed the end-Cretaceous extinction and lived on in the warm Paleocene rivers of North America.

Branisella.note: The oldest known New World monkey, from Bolivia -- descended from African primates that had crossed the Atlantic, probably on floating vegetation.

pbdb.homonym: Branisella, a Silurian-Devonian brachiopod; the monkey is Branisella boliviana Hoffstetter 1969

Champsosaurus.note: A gharial-snouted choristodere -- not a crocodile at all -- that fished the rivers of the latest Cretaceous and Paleocene, and came through the extinction that ended the dinosaurs.

Chriacus.note: A raccoon-sized arctocyonid with a long tail and grasping feet -- a climbing omnivore of the Paleocene forests.

Cinnamomum.note: Cinnamon and camphor laurels, whose three-veined leaves are among the commonest fossils of the warm Paleogene and Miocene forests of Europe and North America; today they grow wild only in tropical and subtropical Asia.

Diplocynodon.note: A small alligator relative, the common crocodilian of Europe's lakes and rivers from the Eocene to the Miocene.

Diplomystus.note: A herring relative of the Eocene lakes of Wyoming, often fossilised with a smaller fish -- Knightia -- in its mouth.
Diplomystus.conf_note: the genus as used here is the Green River D. dentatus; Old World and Cretaceous referrals belong to other ellimmichthyids

Ekaltadeta.note: A 'killer kangaroo': a rat-kangaroo relative with serrated slicing premolars, probably an omnivore that took small animals.

Eosimias.note: A tiny early anthropoid from the Eocene of China, small enough to sit in a hand -- evidence that the monkey-and-ape line began in Asia.

Eritherium.note: The oldest known proboscidean: a fox-sized animal from the Paleocene of Morocco, 55 million years before the mammoths.

Glyptostrobus.note: The Chinese swamp cypress. In the Paleocene and Eocene it lined swamps and coal-forming mires across the northern continents; today a few hundred wild trees survive in southern China, Vietnam and Laos.

Gobiatherium.note: A hornless dinocerate with a big, bulbous snout, from the Middle Eocene of Mongolia.

Heliobatis.note: A freshwater stingray of the Eocene Green River lakes -- a sea animal living far inland.

Heomys.note: A small gnawing mammal from the Paleocene of China, close to the common ancestor of rodents and rabbits.

Heptodon.note: An early tapir the size of a small pony, still without the trunk -- a body plan the line then kept for fifty million years.

Hoplophoneus.note: A leopard-sized nimravid 'false sabre-tooth', with a bony flange on its jaw to guard its long canines.
Hoplophoneus.conf_note: the European referrals are other nimravids (Eusmilus); Hoplophoneus proper is North American

Hyrachyus.note: A tapir-sized, hornless early rhinocerotoid, widespread across the Eocene northern continents.

Hyracodon.note: A long-legged 'running rhinoceros', pony-sized and hornless, built for speed on the open Oligocene plains.

Indohyus.note: A raccoon-sized, chevrotain-like artiodactyl with thick, dense leg bones for wading -- the closest known relative of whales.

Leptictidium.note: A long-tailed, long-snouted insectivore that ran on its hind legs through the undergrowth of the Eocene forests of Europe.

Leptomeryx.note: A small, hornless ruminant like a chevrotain, one of the commonest mammals of the Oligocene plains of North America.

Liquidambar.note: Sweetgums, star-leaved trees that spread across the northern continents in the Paleogene; the ice ages cut them back to three refuges -- eastern North America, south-west Turkey and southern China.

Litokoala.note: An early koala of the Miocene rainforests, smaller than today's and with a less specialised diet.

Mayulestes.note: A weasel-sized early sparassodont, a climbing predator at the root of South America's marsupial-line carnivores.

Mesonyx.note: A wolf-sized mesonychid with hoofed toes and crushing teeth -- a running, hoofed carnivore unlike anything alive.

Mioplosus.note: A perch-like predatory fish of the Green River lakes, sometimes preserved choking on its last meal.

Nambaroo.note: A small early kangaroo that probably bounded on all fours rather than hopping on two feet.

Notharctus.note: A lemur-like adapiform primate of the Eocene forests of Wyoming, leaping between branches with a long tail.

Oxyaena.note: A wolverine-like oxyaenid, one of the first large mammal predators, of the earliest Eocene of North America.

Pakicetus.note: The earliest whale: a wolf-sized, four-legged land animal of the Eocene of Pakistan, with the ear bones that mark every whale since.

Palaeochiropteryx.note: One of the earliest bats: its stomach contents show it hunted moths near the forest floor, and its ear bones show it could echolocate.

Palaeolagus.note: An early rabbit of the White River beds, already almost modern -- the rabbit body plan has barely changed in 35 million years.

Palaeomastodon.note: A long-jawed early proboscidean of the Fayum swamps, with short tusks above and below -- a step between Moeritherium and the mastodons.

Palaeosyops.note: A heavy, hornless brontothere, a browser in the warm Eocene forests before the giant horned kinds.

Palaeotherium.note: A horse relative that looked more like a tapir, from pony- to horse-sized, which browsed the Eocene forests of Europe's islands.

Pantolambda.note: A sheep-sized early pantodont, one of the first mammals to grow large after the dinosaurs -- a heavy-limbed browser of the Paleocene swamp forests.

Patriofelis.note: A lion-sized oxyaenid with a short, heavy skull -- the top predator of the Middle Eocene of Wyoming.

Plesiadapis.note: A squirrel-like relative of primates with big gnawing incisors -- one of the few Paleocene mammals found on both sides of the young North Atlantic.

Pleuraspidotherium.note: A small hoofed mammal of the Paleocene of France, known from hundreds of individuals in a single quarry.

Poebrotherium.note: A goat-sized early camel of the White River plains -- camels began in North America and stayed there for 35 million years.

Presbyornis.note: A long-legged early relative of ducks that nested in vast colonies on the shores of Eocene soda lakes -- a duck's head on a flamingo's body.

Proborhyaena.note: A bear-sized sparassodont, a marsupial-line predator of the Oligocene with ever-growing canines.

Prodinoceras.note: An early dinocerate from the Paleocene of Mongolia and China -- a tapir-sized ancestor of the horned, tusked uintatheres.

Pucadelphys.note: A mouse-sized marsupial relative from the earliest Paleocene of Bolivia, found as groups of complete skeletons -- perhaps families killed together.

Sabal.note: Palmettos: fan palms that grew in the Eocene as far north as southern England and the Pacific Northwest; today they reach only the south-eastern United States, Mexico and the Caribbean.

Saghatherium.note: A small hyrax of the Fayum -- from a time when hyraxes, not antelopes, were Africa's main grazers and browsers.

Stylemys.note: A land tortoise of the Oligocene plains, common enough that its shells weather out of the White River badlands by the hundred.

Subhyracodon.note: A hornless, cow-sized rhinoceros of the White River plains -- North America had rhinos of its own until five million years ago.

Taxodium.note: The bald cypress, whose buttressed trunks and 'knees' stand in swamp water. In the Paleogene it grew across the northern continents; today only in the south-eastern United States and Mexico.

Thomashuxleya.note: A sheep-sized notoungulate -- one of South America's native hoofed mammals, which evolved in isolation for sixty million years.

Titanohyrax.note: A hyrax as heavy as a small rhinoceros, the giant of the hyraxes that then held Africa's plant-eating niches.

Titanoides.note: A bear-sized pantodont with long tusk-like canines and clawed feet -- a Paleocene browser, among the largest mammals of its time.

Wakaleo.note: A dog-sized marsupial lion of the Miocene rainforests of Queensland, with blade-like premolars for slicing meat.
